title: I Have Diabetes and a Small Foot Sore That Won't Heal — How Worried Should I Be?
metaDescription: A foot sore that isn't healing is a diabetic foot problem until proven otherwise. What it means, why numb feet hide injuries, and when to be seen the same week.
intro: It is usually something small: a blister from new chappals, a crack in the heel, a corn that was trimmed at home. The person has diabetes, the foot does not hurt much, so it is left alone for a week, then two. That absence of pain is exactly what makes this situation worth taking seriously. Here is what a sore that isn't healing can mean, what you can do today, and when it should not wait.

sections.heading: How worried should I be about a foot sore that isn't healing?
sections.body:
Take it seriously, but you do not need to panic. In someone with diabetes, a sore that has not clearly improved within a few days should be examined by a doctor rather than watched at home. Most small sores heal when they are seen early and the pressure on them is removed. The risk lies in waiting: the World Health Organization notes that diabetic foot problems can lead to foot ulcers and may lead to amputation.

So the honest answer is: concerned enough to book a review this week, not so alarmed that you stop thinking clearly.

sections.heading: Why does a diabetic foot sore not hurt — and why does that matter?
sections.body:
Because diabetes can damage the nerves in the feet, and a foot that cannot feel pain cannot warn you. The CDC explains that nerve damage can cause you to lose feeling in your feet, and that if you do not feel pain you may not notice a cut, blister or sore.

Two things then compound each other. A numb foot keeps being walked on, so the injury never gets a rest. And WHO also points to poor blood flow in people with diabetes, which slows healing further. A lack of pain therefore tells you nothing about how serious the sore is.

sections.heading: Which signs mean I should be seen the same day?
sections.body: Any of the following with a foot sore means go to a doctor or hospital that day, not next week. The CDC advises against waiting for your next routine appointment when warning signs appear.
bullets: Redness spreading up the foot, new swelling, or the foot feeling warmer than the other one
Pus, a foul smell, or discharge from the sore
Fever, chills, or feeling generally unwell with a foot wound
Skin turning dark, blue or black, or a foot that is cold and pale
A sore where you can see or feel deep tissue or bone

sections.heading: What should I do at home until I am seen?
sections.body:
Keep weight and friction off the sore, keep it clean and covered with a dry dressing, and do not cut it, burst it, or trim a corn or callus yourself. Avoid walking barefoot, even indoors; the CDC advises always wearing shoes and socks or slippers. Check both feet properly, using a mirror or a family member to see the soles. Keep your blood sugar as well controlled as you can, and do not stop your diabetes medicines.

Avoid home remedies such as turmeric paste, hot water soaks, heating pads or ointments applied without advice. A numb foot can be burned without feeling it.

sections.heading: What will the doctor actually check?
sections.body:
Expect a look at the sore itself (size, depth, signs of infection), a test of sensation in the foot, a check of the pulses to judge blood supply, and often an X-ray if bone involvement or a deformity is suspected. Blood tests and a swab may follow.

The IWGDF 2023 prevention guideline recommends that people with diabetes who are at very low risk are screened for loss of protective sensation and peripheral artery disease at least yearly, and those at higher risk more often. If you have never had your feet examined, that gap is worth closing even when you have no sore.

table.caption: What a foot review typically covers, and why. This is a general outline, not a protocol for any individual patient.
rows: The sore: size, depth, edges, colour
Whether it is superficial or deep, and how it is progressing
Signs of infection: warmth, swelling, discharge
How much the foot is protecting itself
Whether blood supply is enough to heal
Bone involvement or deformity that is adding pressure

sections.heading: Will I need surgery?
sections.body:
Often not. Many sores heal with off-loading, regular dressing, infection control and good sugar control. Surgery is considered when there is deep infection, bone involvement, a deformity that keeps creating pressure points, or a wound that fails to improve despite proper care. We cannot judge that without examining the foot, so be wary of anyone who promises either surgery or no surgery over the phone.

A quick note on prevention: the IWGDF guideline advises people at risk to learn proper foot self-care, to avoid walking without suitable foot protection, and, for those at moderate to high risk, to wear properly fitting therapeutic footwear.

faqs.q: Can a diabetic foot ulcer heal on its own?
faqs.a: A small, superficial sore can heal if pressure is taken off it and it is kept clean, but it should still be examined. Reduced sensation and reduced blood flow in diabetes slow healing, so a sore that is not clearly improving within a few days needs assessment rather than waiting.

faqs.q: Why doesn't my diabetic foot sore hurt?
faqs.a: Nerve damage from diabetes can cause loss of feeling in the feet, so you may not notice a cut, blister or sore. Lack of pain does not mean the sore is minor; it often means the foot is not warning you.

faqs.q: When should I go to hospital for a diabetic foot sore?
faqs.a: Go the same day if there is spreading redness, swelling, warmth, pus or a foul smell, fever or feeling unwell, dark or black skin, a cold pale foot, or a sore that looks deep. Do not wait for your next routine appointment.

faqs.q: Should I walk barefoot or use home remedies on the sore?
faqs.a: No. The CDC advises never going barefoot, even indoors. Avoid heat, hot soaks, unprescribed ointments and cutting a corn yourself, because a numb foot can be injured without you feeling it.

faqs.q: How often should people with diabetes have their feet examined?
faqs.a: At least once a year, and more often if there is already nerve damage, poor circulation, a deformity or a past ulcer. The IWGDF 2023 guideline recommends yearly screening even for very low-risk people, and more frequent screening for higher-risk people.
